<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md:12" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/instrumentation.md" title="Instrumentation" section="Instrumentation > How to instrument > Subsystems > Failures">
#### Failures

Failures should be handled similarly to logging. Every time there is a failure, a
counter should be incremented. Unlike logging, the error may also bubble up to a
more general error counter depending on how your code is structured.

When reporting failures, you should generally have some other metric
representing the total number of attempts. This makes the failure ratio easy to calculate.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:33" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Operational Considerations > Common Pitfalls">
### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings
   - Mismatches can cause unnecessary duplicates or missed notifications
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:85" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `sqrt()`">
## `sqrt()`

`sqrt(v instant-vector)` calculates the square root of all float samples in
`v`. Histogram samples in the input vector are ignored silently.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

## Summary

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened">

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

## Per-step stats

- **totalQueryableSamples** / **totalQueryableSamplesPerStep**: Total number of samples *loaded* during the query. For range-vector functions (e.g. `rate`, `sum_over_time`) evaluated over multiple steps, each step counts the full window (the same point may be counted in multiple steps).
- **samplesRead** / **samplesReadPerStep**: Total number of samples *read* (I/O). For range-vector functions in range queries, only *new* points per step are counted (step 0: full window; later steps: points not seen in the previous step). For other query types, this equals totalQueryableSamples.
- **peakSamples**: Peak number of samples in memory during evaluation (used for the `query.max-samples` limit).
</source>

### Common Pitfalls

4. **Unroutable advertise addresses**
   - If `--cluster.advertise-address` is not set, Alertmanager tries to auto-detect
   - The value must be an IP address in `<ip>:<port>` format — **hostnames are not supported**. Using a hostname will log a warning, and startup will continue with the advertise address unset or incorrect, resulting in cluster communication failures
   - For cloud/NAT environments, explicitly set a routable IP address (e.g. `--cluster.advertise-address=192.0.2.1:9094`)

5. **Mismatched cluster configurations**
   - All instances should have the same `--cluster.peer-timeout` and gossip settings

### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

answers:
Based on the incident data and documentation, here are the recurring causes I've identified:

## Incident Patterns

From our incident log, there are 3 incidents with these root causes:

| Incident | Failed Service | Duration | Root Cause |
|----------|----------------|----------|------------|
| INC-2093 | registry-db | 42 min | Disk check failure triggering database failover [D11:1] |
| INC-2067 | kb-search | ~6.5 days | Research agent served stale cached KB articles [D10:0] |
| INC-2041 | auth-service | 2h 15min | Expired intermediate certificate causing gateway timeouts [D09:2] |

## Recurring Causes

**1. Infrastructure Health Events**
- Database disk check failures triggering failovers ([D11:0][D11:1])
- Certificate expiration affecting service connectivity ([D09:2])
- *Pattern*: These cascade into broader outages affecting dependent agents

**2. Data Freshness & Caching Issues**
- Agents serving stale cached data without monitoring for correctness ([D10:0][D10:2])
- Knowledge base updates not reflected in agent responses
- *Pattern*: Monitoring focuses on latency/errors rather than data accuracy

**3. Timeout/Retry Logic Problems**
- Billing agent treated payment gateway timeouts as transient errors and retried excessively until hitting limits
- *Pattern*: Misconfigured retry behavior masking real failures

**4. Alerting Gaps**
- Registry monitoring lost sight of all agents during outage
- No alerts fired for research agent until manual comparison revealed stale answers
- Prometheus default `for` duration too short, causing premature alerts

The most common pattern appears to be **infrastructure-dependent services failing due to health checks or certificate management**, followed by **caching/data consistency issues where agents don't verify result freshness**.

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

Based on the incident data and documentation, here are the recurring causes I've identified:

## Incident Patterns

From our incident log, there are 3 incidents with these root causes:

| Incident | Failed Service | Duration | Root Cause |
|----------|----------------|----------|------------|
| INC-2093 | registry-db | 42 min | Disk check failure triggering database failover [D11:1] |
| INC-2067 | kb-search | ~6.5 days | Research agent served stale cached KB articles [D10:0] |
| INC-2041 | auth-service | 2h 15min | Expired intermediate certificate causing gateway timeouts [D09:2] |

## Recurring Causes

**1. Infrastructure Health Events**
- Database disk check failures triggering failovers ([D11:0][D11:1])
- Certificate expiration affecting service connectivity ([D09:2])
- *Pattern*: These cascade into broader outages affecting dependent agents

**2. Data Freshness & Caching Issues**
- Agents serving stale cached data without monitoring for correctness ([D10:0][D10:2])
- Knowledge base updates not reflected in agent responses
- *Pattern*: Monitoring focuses on latency/errors rather than data accuracy

**3. Timeout/Retry Logic Problems**
- Billing agent treated payment gateway timeouts as transient errors and retried excessively until hitting limits
- *Pattern*: Misconfigured retry behavior masking real failures

**4. Alerting Gaps**
- Registry monitoring lost sight of all agents during outage
- No alerts fired for research agent until manual comparison revealed stale answers
- Prometheus default `for` duration too short, causing premature alerts

The most common pattern appears to be **infrastructure-dependent services failing due to health checks or certificate management**, followed by **caching/data consistency issues where agents don't verify result freshness**.

Based on the incident data and documentation, here are the recurring causes I've identified:

## Incident Patterns

From our incident log, there are 3 incidents with these root causes:

| Incident | Failed Service | Duration | Root Cause |
|----------|----------------|----------|------------|

| INC-2041 | auth-service | 2h 15min | Expired intermediate certificate causing gateway timeouts [D09:2] |

## Recurring Causes

**1. Infrastructure Health Events**
- Database disk check failures triggering failovers ([D11:0][D11:1])
- Certificate expiration affecting service connectivity ([D09:2])
- *Pattern*: These cascade into broader outages affecting dependent agents

**2. Data Freshness & Caching Issues**
- Agents serving stale cached data without monitoring for correctness ([D10:0][D10:2])
- Knowledge base updates not reflected in agent responses
- *Pattern*: Monitoring focuses on latency/errors rather than data accuracy

**3. Timeout/Retry Logic Problems**
- Billing agent treated payment gateway timeouts as transient errors and retried excessively until hitting limits
- *Pattern*: Misconfigured retry behavior masking real failures

**4. Alerting Gaps**
- Registry monitoring lost sight of all agents during outage
- No alerts fired for research agent until manual comparison revealed stale answers
- Prometheus default `for` duration too short, causing premature alerts

The most common pattern appears to be **infrastructure-dependent services failing due to health checks or certificate management**, followed by **caching/data consistency issues where agents don't verify result freshness**.

answers:
Based on our incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## Data Freshness vs. Latency Metrics

The research_agent incident (INC-2067) showed that **standard latency and error rate metrics don't catch content freshness issues** [D10:2]. When knowledge-base articles are cached with long TTLs (7 days instead of 7 hours), searches become instant and never error—but the answers drift out of date over time. The only signal was a user manually comparing an answer with the source.

**Gap**: There's no monitoring measure for whether search results or cached data are current.

## Paging Gaps During Quiet Hours

During the billing_agent incident (INC-2041), error-rate alerts (`AgentErrorRateHigh`) fired at 06:02, but were not pageable because they occurred outside business hours (08:00-20:00) [D08:1][D15:4]. This delayed discovery until the next morning at 08:00, giving us 2+ hours of unnotified failures.

**Gap**: Only `RegistryUnreachable` alerts page during quiet hours; agent health alerts are delayed until morning.

## Agent Loss During Infrastructure Outages

During the registry database failover (INC-2093), monitoring **"lost sight of every agent"** for 42 minutes while registry-api was unavailable [D11:0]. Without the registry, we couldn't see agent health at all.

**Gap**: Agent visibility is completely lost during registry outages, even though the outage itself might be brief and transient.

## Deep Dependency Chain Visibility

The billing_agent incident revealed authentication failures deep in the dependency chain (payments-gateway → auth-service → certificate renewal) [D09:1]. We saw the billing agent errors first, but didn't immediately understand the root cause without digging deeper.

**Gap**: Indirect service failures may not surface quickly through agent-level monitoring alone.

These gaps led to concrete improvements: kb-search cache settings now require approval for TTLs above 24 hours, each result carries an update timestamp, and monitoring now shows the last good agent list during registry outages rather than showing nothing [D10:3][D11:3].

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are

content.text:
Based on our incident history, here are the key monitoring gaps that incidents have exposed:

## Data Freshness vs. Latency Metrics

The research_agent incident (INC-2067) showed that **standard latency and error rate metrics don't catch content freshness issues** [D10:2]. When knowledge-base articles are cached with long TTLs (7 days instead of 7 hours), searches become instant and never error—but the answers drift out of date over time. The only signal was a user manually comparing an answer with the source.

**Gap**: There's no monitoring measure for whether search results or cached data are current.

## Paging Gaps During Quiet Hours

During the billing_agent incident (INC-2041), error-rate alerts (`AgentErrorRateHigh`) fired at 06:02, but were not pageable because they occurred outside business hours (08:00-20:00) [D08:1][D15:4]. This delayed discovery until the next morning at 08:00, giving us 2+ hours of unnotified failures.

**Gap**: Only `RegistryUnreachable` alerts page during quiet hours; agent health alerts are delayed until morning.

## Agent Loss During Infrastructure Outages

During the registry database failover (INC-2093), monitoring **"lost sight of every agent"** for 42 minutes while registry-api was unavailable [D11:0]. Without the registry, we couldn't see agent health at all.

**Gap**: Agent visibility is completely lost during registry outages, even though the outage itself might be brief and transient.

## Deep Dependency Chain Visibility

The billing_agent incident revealed authentication failures deep in the dependency chain (payments-gateway → auth-service → certificate renewal) [D09:1]. We saw the billing agent errors first, but didn't immediately understand the root cause without digging deeper.

**Gap**: Indirect service failures may not surface quickly through agent-level monitoring alone.

These gaps led to concrete improvements: kb-search cache settings now require approval for TTLs above 24 hours, each result carries an update timestamp, and monitoring now shows the last good agent list during registry outages rather than showing nothing [D10:3][D11:3].

This made it impossible to determine which agents were actually affected or identify new issues. We now keep the last good agent list when the registry is unreachable [D11:3].

## **Standby/Replication Health**
During INC-2093, the standby database fell **38 minutes behind the primary**, but there was **no alert** on replication lag. Standby systems should trigger alerts when they fall more than 60 seconds behind the primary [D11:3].

## **Cache Freshness**
In INC-2067, kb-search's cache TTL was increased from 7 hours to 7 days without proper review or approval, causing cached content to drift significantly out of date. Every search returned old article versions, and responses became progressively stale each day. We now require Search team approval for TTL changes over 24 hours, and results include update timestamps [D10:3].

## **Pager Coverage**
For INC-2041, an `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired for `billing_agent` but **no one was paged** because it occurred outside normal paging hours. There was no mechanism to ensure critical agent health alerts reach on-call coverage.

## **Dependent Service Failures**
The `billing_agent` was stuck waiting on connections to the payments-gateway, and the underlying certificate renewal with auth-service never triggered an alert until manually investigated. Inter-agent dependencies and external service connectivity aren't being proactively monitored.

These gaps highlight that we need better cross-dependency monitoring, fallback agent discovery, and stricter change management for caching/configurations that affect accuracy-critical services.

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%

</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

Based on the incident data and documentation, our incidents have exposed several key monitoring gaps:

## **Agent Discovery & Status**
When the registry is unreachable (as in INC-2093), **monitoring shows no agents at all** instead of maintaining the last known state. This made it impossible to determine which agents were actually affected or identify new issues. We now keep the last good agent list when the registry is unreachable [D11:3].

## **Standby/Replication Health**
During INC-2093, the standby database fell **38 minutes behind the primary**, but there was **no alert** on replication lag. Standby systems should trigger alerts when they fall more than 60 seconds behind the primary [D11:3].

## **Cache Freshness**
In INC-2067, kb-search's cache TTL was increased from 7 hours to 7 days without proper review or approval, causing cached content to drift significantly out of date. Every search returned old article versions, and responses became progressively stale each day. We now require Search team approval for TTL changes over 24 hours, and results include update timestamps [D10:3].

## **Pager Coverage**
For INC-2041, an `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired for `billing_agent` but **no one was paged** because it occurred outside normal paging hours. There was no mechanism to ensure critical agent health alerts reach on-call coverage.

## **Dependent Service Failures**
The `billing_agent` was stuck waiting on connections to the payments-gateway, and the underlying certificate renewal with auth-service never triggered an alert until manually investigated. Inter-agent dependencies and external service connectivity aren't being proactively monitored.

These gaps highlight that we need better cross-dependency monitoring, fallback agent discovery, and stricter change management for caching/configurations that affect accuracy-critical services.

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%
accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as
the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a
case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the
data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.

## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:3" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Online serving systems">
### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/alerting.md" title="Alerting" section="Alerting > What to alert on > Batch jobs">
### Batch jobs

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

This should generally be at least enough time for 2 full runs of the batch job.
For a job that runs every 4 hours and takes an hour, 10 hours would be a
reasonable threshold. If you cannot withstand a single run failing, run the
job more frequently, as a single failure should not require human intervention.
</source>

## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%
accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as
the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a

data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.

### Online serving systems

Typically alert on high latency and error rates as high up in the stack as possible.

Only page on latency at one point in a stack. If a lower-level component is
slower than it should be, but the overall user latency is fine, then there is
no need to page.

For error rates, page on user-visible errors. If there are errors further down
the stack that will cause such a failure, there is no need to page on them
separately. However, if some failures are not user-visible, but are otherwise
severe enough to require human involvement (for example, you are losing a lot of
money), add pages to be sent on those.
</source>

For batch jobs it makes sense to page if the batch job has not succeeded
recently enough, and this will cause user-visible problems.

<source id="prometheus-server/prometheus_agent.md:1" doc="prometheus-server/prometheus_agent.md" title="Prometheus Agent Mode" section="Prometheus Agent Mode > Prometheus Agent Mode">
## Prometheus Agent Mode

With Remote Write, Prometheus still uses a pull model to gather metrics from applications, which gives us an understanding of those different failure modes. After that, we batch samples and series and export, replicate (push) data to the Remote Write endpoints, limiting the number of monitoring unknowns that the central point has.
Streaming data from such a scraper enables Global View use cases by allowing you to store metrics data in a centralized location. This enables the separation of concerns, which is useful when different teams manage applications than the observability or monitoring pipelines. 
</source>

<source id="D07:2" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Step 1: Check the target is allowed">
## Step 1: Check the target is allowed

Both target models are allowed on the `standard` tier, so neither agent needs a tier change. If you'd rather move to `claude-opus`, the agent must move to the `priority` tier first, or the change fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D02:1" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Request errors">
## Request errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |
| `REG-1010` | `MODEL_DEPRECATED` | 422 | The model is deprecated and can't be newly assigned. Currently applies to `claude-legacy`. |
</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md:8" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md" title="Overview" section="Overview > When does it not fit?">
## When does it not fit?

Prometheus values reliability. You can always view what statistics are
available about your system, even under failure conditions. If you need 100%
accuracy, such as for per-request billing, Prometheus is not a good choice, as
the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough. In such a
case, you would be best off using some other system to collect and analyze the
data for billing, and Prometheus for the rest of your monitoring.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:18" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Split-Brain Handling (Fail Open) > Behavior During Partition">
### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

With Remote Write, Prometheus still uses a pull model to gather metrics from applications, which gives us an understanding of those different failure modes. After that, we batch samples and series and export, replicate (push) data to the Remote Write endpoints, limiting the number of monitoring unknowns that the central point has.

<source id="D02:1" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Request errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Request errors

| Code | Name | HTTP | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REG-1005` | `AGENT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No agent has this `agent_id`. Ids are case-sensitive. |
| `REG-1006` | `AGENT_NAME_TAKEN` | 409 | An agent with this `agent_id` already exists, including a retired one. |
| `REG-1007` | `MODEL_NOT_ALLOWED` | 422 | The model isn't on the allowlist for the agent's tier. Change the tier first, or pick an allowed model. |
| `REG-1008` | `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | The body is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type. The message names the field. |

</source>

<source id="D01:4" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Creating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Creating an agent

`POST /agents` creates an agent. It needs a `write` key. The body must include `agent_id`, `model`, `tier` and `owner`; `status` defaults to `active`.

```json
{"agent_id": "triage_agent", "model": "claude-haiku", "tier": "standard", "owner": "support-team"}
```

Agent ids must be unique: reusing one returns `REG-1006`. The model must be allowed on the agent's tier (see "Tiers and models"), or the request fails with `REG-1007`.
</source>

<source id="D14:1" doc="D14" title="Agent owners' FAQ" section="Agent owners' FAQ > Can my agent use the biggest model?" date="2026-09-10" type="official">
## Can my agent use the biggest model?

Only on the priority tier. Standard-tier agents can use the smaller and mid-sized models. Moving to priority needs a sign-off from whoever holds your team's budget, and after that you can change the model.
</source>

<source id="D01:5" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Updating an agent" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Updating an agent

`PATCH /agents/{agent_id}` changes one or more of `model`, `tier`, `owner` and `status`. Send only the fields you're changing. It needs a `write` key; a `read` key gets `REG-1004`.

```bash
curl -X PATCH https://registry.internal.example/v2/agents/research_agent \
  -H "X-Registry-Key: $REGISTRY_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "claude-sonnet"}'
```

A change takes effect on the agent's next session, not in the middle of one that's running. Setting `status` to `paused` stops new sessions from starting; `retired` also hides the agent from the default listing.
</source>

<source id="alertmanager/high_availability.md:18" doc="alertmanager/high_availability.md" title="High Availability" section="High Availability > Split-Brain Handling (Fail Open) > Behavior During Partition" date="2026-09-27" type="vendor">
### Behavior During Partition

**In Partition A** (AM-1 alone):
- AM-1 sees itself as position 0
- Waits 0 × timeout = 0 seconds
- Sends notifications (no dedup from AM-2/AM-3)

**In Partition B** (AM-2, AM-3):
- AM-2 is position 0, AM-3 is position 1
- AM-2 waits 0 seconds, sends notification
- AM-3 sees AM-2's notification log entry, deduplicates

**Result**: Duplicate notifications sent (one from Partition A, one from Partition B)

This is **intentional** - Alertmanager prefers duplicate notifications over missed alerts.
</source>

Based on our incidents and incident reports, here are the key monitoring gaps we've exposed:

### 1. **No Freshness/Validity Checks** ([D10:2])
**Incident INC-2067**: The `research_agent` returned outdated knowledge-base articles for a week because:
- Monitoring only tracked latency and error rates
- Cached answers were "fast and never failed," appearing perfectly healthy in metrics
- Nothing measured whether results were current or stale
- Detection relied entirely on manual comparison by users

### 2. **Late Failure Detection** ([D09:2][D09:1])
**Incident INC-2041**: A billing agent outage lasted ~50 minutes with delayed detection:
- Certificate expired at 06:00, but monitoring systems didn't track auth-service health continuously
- `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired at 06:02 but didn't page because it was outside paging hours (08:00-20:00)
- On-call engineer had to investigate manually at 08:00 to understand what happened

### 3. **No Infrastructure Dependency Monitoring** ([D11:2])
**Incident INC-2093**: A 42-minute registry outage during database failover:
- No alerts triggered when the standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary
- Monitoring lost sight of **every agent** during the outage, making it impossible to identify which services were impacted
- The on-call engineer couldn't prioritize remediation without visibility

### Summary of Key Gaps:
| Gap | What Was Missing | Impact |
|-----|-----------------|--------|
| Data freshness | No checks for cache validity, TTLs, content currency | Outdated responses served silently |
| Dependency monitoring | No awareness of upstream service health (auth-service certificates) | Cascading failures undetected |
| Infrastructure resilience | No lag alerts between primary/standby databases | Blind spots during recoveries |
| Paging coverage | Error rate alerts outside business hours | Late detection window |

The docs recommend supplementing whitebox monitoring with external blackbox monitoring to catch problems otherwise invisible [D08:1].

### Metamonitoring

It is important to have confidence that monitoring is working. Accordingly, have
alerts to ensure that Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways, and
other monitoring infrastructure are available and running correctly.

As always, if it is possible to alert on symptoms rather than causes, this helps
to reduce noise. For example, a blackbox test that alerts are getting from
PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than individual
alerts on each.

Supplementing the whitebox monitoring of Prometheus with external blackbox
monitoring can catch problems that are otherwise invisible, and also serves as
a fallback in case internal systems completely fail.
</source>

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.

<source id="D10:0" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Summary">
## Summary

From 2026-06-15 to 2026-06-22, `research_agent` answered questions with knowledge-base articles that had since been updated. Nothing failed and no alert fired; a user noticed that a report quoted a policy that had changed four days earlier.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D07:1" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Which agents are affected">
## Which agents are affected

As of this writing, two active agents are on `claude-legacy`:

| Agent | Owner | Target model |
|---|---|---|
| `research_agent` | research-team | `claude-sonnet` |
| `notes_agent` | support-team | `claude-haiku` |

Owners can check any agent with `GET /agents/{agent_id}` and look at its `model` field.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact">
## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

Alerts go to the on-call channel and page the on-call engineer between 08:00 and 20:00. Outside those hours, only `RegistryUnreachable` pages.
</source>

<source id="D02:3" doc="D02" title="Error code reference" section="Error code reference > Monitoring errors" date="2026-08-18" type="official">
## Monitoring errors

These come from the monitoring service, not from the Registry API, but they appear in the same alert channels.

| Code | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MON-2001` | `SCRAPE_FAILED` | Monitoring couldn't collect metrics from one agent. Usually the agent is paused or restarting. |
| `MON-2002` | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE` | Monitoring failed to reach the Registry API three times in a row. It raises the `RegistryUnreachable` alert. |
</source>

<source id="D10:2" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Why it took a week to notice" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Why it took a week to notice

The agent's latency and error rate looked better than usual: cached answers are fast and never fail. Nothing in monitoring measures whether results are current. The only signal was a person comparing an answer with the source.
</source>

<source id="D10:0" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > Summary" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## Summary

From 2026-06-15 to 2026-06-22, `research_agent` answered questions with knowledge-base articles that had since been updated. Nothing failed and no alert fired; a user noticed that a report quoted a policy that had changed four days earlier.
</source>

<source id="D10:1" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What happened" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What happened

`research_agent` finds its sources through kb-search. On 2026-06-15 a config change set the kb-search cache's time-to-live to 7 days instead of 7 hours. Every search that had been cached returned the version of each article from when it was first cached, so answers drifted further out of date each day.
</source>

<source id="D10:3" doc="D10" title="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results" section="Incident INC-2067: research_agent returning outdated results > What we changed" date="2026-06-24" type="official">
## What we changed

- kb-search's cache settings are now reviewed like code, and a time-to-live above 24 hours needs the Search team's approval.
- Each kb-search result now carries the date the article was last updated, and `research_agent` includes it when it cites a source.
- Reports produced during the affected week were flagged to their readers.
</source>

<source id="D07:1" doc="D07" title="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy" section="Runbook: migrating agents off claude-legacy > Which agents are affected" date="2026-07-02" type="official">
## Which agents are affected

As of this writing, two active agents are on `claude-legacy`:

| Agent | Owner | Target model |
|---|---|---|
| `research_agent` | research-team | `claude-sonnet` |
| `notes_agent` | support-team | `claude-haiku` |

Owners can check any agent with `GET /agents/{agent_id}` and look at its `model` field.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D04:2" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > How requests flow" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## How requests flow

When a request reaches registry-api, it first asks auth-service to validate the `X-Registry-Key` header, then reads or writes registry-db. If auth-service is slow, every registry request is slow; if registry-db is unavailable, registry-api can't answer at all.

Monitoring gets its list of agents from registry-api every 30 seconds, then collects metrics from each agent on the list.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="D04:4" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Who to contact" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Who to contact

Page the owning team through the on-call rota: Platform for registry-api and registry-db, Identity for auth-service, Observability for monitoring, and Search for kb-search.
</source>

<source id="D11:2" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What made it worse" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What made it worse

The failover should have taken about 5 minutes. It took 42 because the standby had fallen 38 minutes behind the primary, and nothing alerted on that lag. For the whole outage, monitoring showed no agents at all, so the on-call engineer couldn't tell which agents were affected. Its agent list comes from the registry.
</source>

<source id="D11:1" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Timeline" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Timeline

- 14:10 — The primary registry-db host failed a disk check and failover started.
- 14:11 — `RegistryUnreachable` fired and paged the on-call engineer. The overview dashboard went blank.
- 14:20 — `support_agent` sessions began failing on their first registry lookup. `triage_agent` kept running but couldn't hand tickets over, so 212 tickets queued.
- 14:52 — The standby finished catching up and registry-api recovered. The queued tickets were handed over by 15:05.
</source>

<source id="D11:0" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > Summary" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-08-27, registry-api was unavailable for 42 minutes while registry-db failed over to its standby. Agents that look things up in the registry couldn't finish their tasks, and monitoring lost sight of every agent for the same period.
</source>

<source id="D11:3" doc="D11" title="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover" section="Incident INC-2093: registry outage during database failover > What we changed" date="2026-08-29" type="official">
## What we changed

- An alert now fires when the standby falls more than 60 seconds behind.
- Monitoring keeps its last good agent list when the registry is unreachable, instead of showing nothing.
- `support_agent` now tells users the registry is unavailable instead of failing silently.
</source>

<source id="D04:1" doc="D04" title="Agent platform architecture overview" section="Agent platform architecture overview > Core services" date="2026-02-14" type="official">
## Core services

- **registry-api** — the Registry API. Stores every agent's configuration. Owned by the Platform team.
- **registry-db** — the Postgres database behind registry-api, with a hot standby for failover. Owned by the Platform team.
- **auth-service** — validates registry keys and issues the internal certificates services use to talk to each other. Owned by the Identity team.
- **monitoring** — collects latency and error metrics for every agent and raises alerts. Owned by the Observability team.
- **kb-search** — search over the internal knowledge base, with a response cache in front of it. Owned by the Search team.
</source>

Based on our incidents and incident reports, here are the key monitoring gaps we've exposed:

### 1. **No Freshness/Validity Checks** ([D10:2])
**Incident INC-2067**: The `research_agent` returned outdated knowledge-base articles for a week because:
- Monitoring only tracked latency and error rates
- Cached answers were "fast and never failed," appearing perfectly healthy in metrics
- Nothing measured whether results were current or stale
- Detection relied entirely on manual comparison by users

### 2. **Late Failure Detection** ([D09:2][D09:1])
**Incident INC-2041**: A billing agent outage lasted ~50 minutes with delayed detection:
- Certificate expired at 06:00, but monitoring systems didn't track auth-service health continuously
- `AgentErrorRateHigh` alert fired at 06:02 but didn't page because it was outside paging hours (08:00-20:00)
- On-call engineer had to investigate manually at 08:00 to understand what happened

### 3. **No Infrastructure Dependency Monitoring** ([D11:2])
**Incident INC-2093**: A 42-minute registry outage during database failover:
- No alerts triggered when the standby database fell 38 minutes behind the primary
- Monitoring lost sight of **every agent** during the outage, making it impossible to identify which services were impacted
- The on-call engineer couldn't prioritize remediation without visibility

### Summary of Key Gaps:
| Gap | What Was Missing | Impact |
|-----|-----------------|--------|
| Data freshness | No checks for cache validity, TTLs, content currency | Outdated responses served silently |
| Dependency monitoring | No awareness of upstream service health (auth-service certificates) | Cascading failures undetected |
| Infrastructure resilience | No lag alerts between primary/standby databases | Blind spots during recoveries |
| Paging coverage | Error rate alerts outside business hours | Late detection window |

The docs recommend supplementing whitebox monitoring with external blackbox monitoring to catch problems otherwise invisible [D08:1].

Based on the registry documentation, the current rate limit is **60 requests per minute per key**.

Here are the key details:

- **Rate**: 60 requests per minute per key
- **Error code**: When exceeded, requests receive HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header indicating how many seconds to wait

<source id="D01:8" doc="D01" title="Registry API reference" section="Registry API reference > Rate limits">
## Rate limits

Each key may make 60 requests per minute. Requests past the limit get HTTP 429 with error `REG-1009` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Limits apply per key, not per agent, so two processes sharing one key share one limit.
</source>

<source id="D03:2" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.4 — 2026-05-12">
## v2.4 — 2026-05-12

- Lowered the rate limit from 100 to 60 requests per minute per key. Some internal dashboards were polling hard enough to slow the registry for agents.
- Rate-limited responses (`REG-1009`) now include a `Retry-After` header.
</source>

<source id="D08:4" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > Polling the registry from your own dashboards">
## Polling the registry from your own dashboards

If you build your own dashboard on top of the registry, poll no more than once every few seconds. The registry allows 100 requests per minute per key, and a dashboard that uses most of that leaves nothing for the agent sharing its key.
</source>

<source id="D03:4" doc="D03" title="Registry changelog" section="Registry changelog > v2.2 — 2026-01-20">
## v2.2 — 2026-01-20

- `GET /agents` now pages with `cursor` and `next_cursor`. The `offset` parameter still works but is deprecated.
- Page size is set with `limit`: default 20, maximum 100.
</source>

<source id="D08:0" doc="D08" title="Monitoring guide" section="Monitoring guide > What monitoring collects">
## What monitoring collects

For every agent, monitoring records response time (as p50 and p95), error rate, and the number of sessions. It learns which agents exist by asking the registry for the agent list every 30 seconds, so a new agent appears on the dashboards within a minute of being created.
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md:6" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md" title="Overview" section="Overview > What is Prometheus? > Architecture">
### Architecture

This diagram illustrates the architecture of Prometheus and some of
its ecosystem components:

Prometheus scrapes metrics from instrumented jobs, either directly or via an
intermediary push gateway for short-lived jobs. It stores all scraped samples
locally and runs rules over this data to either aggregate and record new time
series from existing data or generate alerts. Grafana or
other API consumers can be used to visualize the collected data.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md:5" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md" title="Overview" section="Overview > What is Prometheus? > Components">
### Components

The Prometheus ecosystem consists of multiple components, many of which are
optional:

* the main Prometheus server which scrapes and stores time series data
* client libraries for instrumenting application code
* a push gateway for supporting short-lived jobs
* special-purpose exporters for services like HAProxy, StatsD, Graphite, etc.
* an alertmanager to handle alerts
* various support tools

Most Prometheus components are written in Go, making
them easy to build and deploy as static binaries.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md:2" doc="prometheus-docs/introduction/overview.md" title="Overview" section="Overview > What is Prometheus? > Features">
### Features

Prometheus's main features are:

* a multi-dimensional data model with time series data identified by metric name and key/value pairs
* PromQL, a flexible query language
  to leverage this dimensionality
* no reliance on distributed storage; single server nodes are autonomous
* time series collection happens via a pull model over HTTP
* pushing time series is supported via an intermediary gateway
* targets are discovered via service discovery or static configuration
* multiple modes of graphing and dashboarding support
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:9" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Reliability">
## Reliability

When the operating system sends a write request to the storage hardware, there is little it can do to make sure the data has arrived at a truly non-volatile storage area. Rather, it is the administrator's responsibility to make certain that all storage components ensure integrity for both data and file-system metadata. Avoid disk controllers that have non-battery-backed write caches. At the drive level, disable write-back caching if the drive cannot guarantee the data will be written before shutdown. If you use SSDs, be aware that many of these do not honor cache flush commands by default. You can test for reliable I/O subsystem behavior using `diskchecker.pl`.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:74" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability">
#### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/operating/security.md:23" doc="prometheus-docs/operating/security.md" title="Security model" section="Security model > Denial of Service">
## Denial of Service

That said, there are cases where a fix is still worthwhile and a public issue or
pull request is welcome. A good example is a logic bug where an attacker-controlled
length field is trusted without validation and then used to allocate memory — this
is a meaningful improvement to resource safety even if it does not rise to the
level of a private security report. On the other hand, the absence of arbitrary
sanity limits in some part of the code base is generally not worth a report on
its own.

Beyond the scenario of a malicious attack, it is the responsibility of the user to
ensure they provide components with sufficient resources including CPU, RAM, disk
space, IOPS, file descriptors, and bandwidth.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md:40" doc="prometheus-docs/practices/histograms.md" title="Histograms and summaries" section="Histograms and summaries > Quantiles">
## Quantiles

with a number of instances, you will collect request durations from every
single one of them, and then you want to aggregate everything into an overall
95th percentile. However, aggregating the precomputed quantiles from a summary
rarely makes sense. In this particular case, averaging the quantiles yields
statistically nonsensical values.

    avg(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) // BAD!

Using histograms, the aggregation is perfectly possible with the
`histogram_quantile()`
function.

Native histogram version (including NHCB):

    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds[5m]))) // GOOD.

Classic histogram version:

    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) // GOOD.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/operators.md:12" doc="prometheus-server/querying/operators.md" title="Operators" section="Operators > Binary operators > Histogram trim operators">
### Histogram trim operators

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `</` (trim upper): removes all observations above a threshold value
* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

Histogram trim operators are defined between vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs,
where the left hand side is a native histogram (either exponential or NHCB),
and the right hand side is a float threshold value.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md:41" doc="prometheus-server/querying/functions.md" title="Query functions" section="Query functions > `histogram_quantiles()`">
## `histogram_quantiles()`

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag
`--enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions`.**

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤
φ ≤ 1) from a classic
histogram or from
a native histogram. Quantile calculation works the same way as in `histogram_quantile()`.
The second argument (a string) specifies the label name that is used to identify different quantiles in the query result.
```
histogram_quantiles(sum(rate(foo[1m])), "quantile", 0.9, 0.99)
# => {quantile="0.9"} 123
     {quantile="0.99"} 128
```
</source>

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline" date="2026-04-10" type="official">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

That said, there are cases where a fix is still worthwhile and a public issue or
pull request is welcome. A good example is a logic bug where an attacker-controlled
length field is trusted without validation and then used to allocate memory — this
is a meaningful improvement to resource safety even if it does not rise to the
level of a private security report. On the other hand, the absence of arbitrary
sanity limits in some part of the code base is generally not worth a report on
its own.

Beyond the scenario of a malicious attack, it is the responsibility of the user to
ensure they provide components with sufficient resources including CPU, RAM, disk
space, IOPS, file descriptors, and bandwidth.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/wal.md:9" doc="postgresql/wal.md" title="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log" section="Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log > Reliability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
## Reliability

When the operating system sends a write request to the storage hardware, there is little it can do to make sure the data has arrived at a truly non-volatile storage area. Rather, it is the administrator's responsibility to make certain that all storage components ensure integrity for both data and file-system metadata. Avoid disk controllers that have non-battery-backed write caches. At the drive level, disable write-back caching if the drive cannot guarantee the data will be written before shutdown. If you use SSDs, be aware that many of these do not honor cache flush commands by default. You can test for reliable I/O subsystem behavior using `diskchecker.pl`.
</source>

<source id="postgresql/high-availability.md:74" doc="postgresql/high-availability.md" title="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication" section="High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers > Synchronous Replication > Planning for High Availability" date="2026-09-28" type="vendor">
#### Planning for High Availability

If primary restarts while commits are waiting for acknowledgment, those waiting transactions will be marked fully committed once the primary database recovers. There is no way to be certain that all standbys have received all outstanding WAL data at time of the crash of the primary. Some transactions may not show as committed on the standby, even though they show as committed on the primary. The guarantee we offer is that the application will not receive explicit acknowledgment of the successful commit of a transaction until the WAL data is known to be safely received by all the synchronous standbys.
</source>

## Quantiles

with a number of instances, you will collect request durations from every
single one of them, and then you want to aggregate everything into an overall
95th percentile. However, aggregating the precomputed quantiles from a summary
rarely makes sense. In this particular case, averaging the quantiles yields
statistically nonsensical values.

    avg(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) // BAD!

Using histograms, the aggregation is perfectly possible with the
`histogram_quantile()`
function.

Native histogram version (including NHCB):

    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds[5m]))) // GOOD.

Classic histogram version:

    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) // GOOD.
</source>

### Histogram trim operators

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `</` (trim upper): removes all observations above a threshold value
* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

Histogram trim operators are defined between vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs,
where the left hand side is a native histogram (either exponential or NHCB),
and the right hand side is a float threshold value.
</source>

**This function has to be enabled via the feature
flag

`histogram_quantiles(v instant-vector, quantile_label string, φ_1 scalar, φ_2 scalar, ...)` calculates multiple (between 1 and 10) φ-quantiles (0 ≤

<source id="D09:2" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Root cause">
## Root cause

payments-gateway checks every request's certificate with auth-service before it will talk to a caller. An intermediate certificate in auth-service expired at 06:00, so every check failed, and payments-gateway timed out instead of returning an error. `billing_agent` treated the timeouts as transient and retried each one until its step limit ran out.
</source>

<source id="D09:0" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Summary">
## Summary

On 2026-04-08, `billing_agent` failed to issue invoices for 2 hours 15 minutes. Every attempt ended in a timeout from payments-gateway. No customer was charged twice, but 1,140 invoices went out late.
</source>

<source id="D09:3" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > What we changed">
## What we changed

- auth-service now alerts 30 days before any certificate expires.
- payments-gateway now returns an error immediately when a certificate check fails, instead of hanging.
- `billing_agent` stops retrying after three timeouts from the same service in one session.
</source>

<source id="D09:1" doc="D09" title="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices" section="Incident INC-2041: billing_agent unable to issue invoices > Timeline">
## Timeline

- 06:02 — `AgentErrorRateHigh` fired for `billing_agent`. No page: it was outside paging hours.
- 08:00 — The on-call engineer saw the alert and found every failed session stuck on the same payments-gateway call.
- 08:40 — The Payments team found that payments-gateway couldn't open connections to auth-service.
- 08:55 — The Identity team renewed the certificate. `billing_agent` recovered within two minutes.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/operators.md:12" doc="prometheus-server/querying/operators.md" title="Operators" section="Operators > Binary operators > Histogram trim operators">
### Histogram trim operators

The following binary histogram trim operators exist in Prometheus:

* `</` (trim upper): removes all observations above a threshold value
* `>/` (trim lower): removes all observations below a threshold value

Histogram trim operators are defined between vector/scalar and vector/vector value pairs,
where the left hand side is a native histogram (either exponential or NHCB),
and the right hand side is a float threshold value.
</source>

<source id="prometheus-server/querying/operators.md:13" doc="prometheus-server/querying/operators.md" title="Operators" section="Operators > Binary operators > Histogram trim operators">
### Histogram trim operators

In case the threshold value is not aligned to one of the bucket boundaries of the histogram,
either linear (for NHCB and zero buckets of exponential histogram) or exponential (for non zero
bucket of exponential histogram) interpolation is applied to compute the estimated count
of observations that remain in the bucket containing the threshold.

In case when some observations get trimmed, the new sum of observation values is recomputed
(approximately) based on the remaining observations.
</source>

## Naming
